source_text:
De eo igitur, inquit, frater dilectissime Pattici, quod mihi significasti dicens nosse te cupere, cuiusmodi sit natiuitas Adae et Euae, utrum uerbo sint idem prolati, an progeniti ei corpore, respondebitur tibi, ut congruit. namque de his a plerisque in uariis scripturis reuela tionibus que dissimili modo insertum atque commemoratum est. quapropter ueritas istius rei ut sese habet. ab uniuersis fere gentibus ignoratur et ab omnibus. qui etiam de hoc diu multumque disputarunt. si enim illis super Adae et Euae generatione prouenisset manifesto cognoscere. numquam corruptioni et morti subiacerent. manifestam ergo cognitionem huius rei nobis pollicetur, ne corruptioni ac morti subiciamur. et si adhuc parum est, uide, quid sequatur. necessario ergo, inquit, plura sunt ante commemoranda ut ad istud mysterium sine ulla possit ambiguitate perueniri. hoc est, quod dicebam, sic mihi demonstrari debere ueritatem, ut ad eandem sine ulla ambiguitate perueniam. quod si ipse non polliceretur, me tamen hoc exigere et flagitare oportebat, ut tanta mercede cognitionis euidentissimae atque certissimae ex catholico christiano quibuslibet contradicentibus Manichaeum me fieri non puderet. iam igitur audiamus, quid adferat.
Unde si tibi uidetur, inquit, ausculta prius, quae fuerint ante constitutionem mundi et quo pacto proelium sit agitatum, ut possis luminis seiungere naturam ac tenebrarum. iam incredibilia et omnino falsa proposuit. quis enim credat ante constitutionem mundi ullum proelium fuisse commissum? et tamen si esset credibile, modo nos non credere. sed cognoscere uelimus. nam qui dicit Persas et Scythas ante multos annos secum bellasse, rem dicit credibilem, eam tamen, quam uel auditam uel lectam possumus credere, non expertam conprehensamque cognoscere. cum ergo istum repudiarem, si tale aliquid diceret — non enim ea promisit, quae cogerer credere, sed quae possem sine ulla ambiguitate cognoscere —, quomodo eum non repudiabo, quando non modo incerta dicit, sed etiam incredibilia ? sed quid? si aliquibus rationibus ea perspicua et cognita faciet? audiamus ergo, si possumus, cum tota patientia et lenitate. quod sequitur. -!
thought_title: Mani's promise of certain knowledge about Adam and Eve
orientation: Augustine has just finished quoting the opening wishes of Mani's Fundamental Letter and now turns to Mani's central promise of certain knowledge, quoting Mani's reply to Patticus about the birth of Adam and Eve.
pass_a_gloss: Concerning that matter therefore, he says, most beloved brother Patticus, which you indicated to me by saying that you desire to know, of what sort the birth of Adam and Eve is, whether they were brought forth by word as the same, or begotten from his body, it will be answered to you, as is fitting. For about these things by many people in various scriptures and revelations it has been inserted and recorded in a dissimilar manner. Wherefore the truth of this matter, as it has itself, is unknown by almost all nations and by all who even about this have disputed long and much. For if it had come about for them to know clearly about the generation of Adam and Eve, never would they be subject to corruption and death. Therefore he promises to us the clear knowledge of this matter, so that we may not be subjected to corruption and death. And if this is still too little, see what follows. Therefore it is necessary, he says, that more things be recounted beforehand so that one may arrive at this mystery without any ambiguity. This is what I was saying, that the truth ought to be demonstrated to me in such a way that I may arrive at it without any ambiguity. But if he himself did not promise it, nevertheless it was fitting for me to demand and insist upon this, so that with so great a reward of most evident and most certain knowledge I would not be ashamed to become a Manichaean from a Catholic Christian, no matter who contradicted. Now therefore let us hear what he brings forward. Wherefore if it seems good to you, he says, listen first to what things were before the constitution of the world and in what manner the battle was waged, so that you may be able to separate the nature of light and of darkness. Now he has proposed unbelievable and altogether false things. For who would believe that before the constitution of the world any battle was waged? And yet if it were believable, now we do not wish to believe, but to know. For he who says that the Persians and Scythians waged war with each other many years ago, says a believable thing, but that thing, which we can believe either heard or read, we cannot know as experienced and grasped. Therefore when I would reject him, if he said something of such a kind — for he did not promise those things which I would be compelled to believe, but those which I could know without any ambiguity —, how shall I not reject him, when he says not only uncertain things, but even unbelievable things? But what? What if by some reasonings he will make those things clear and known? Let us hear therefore, if we can, with all patience and gentleness, what follows.

choices.term: uerbo sint idem prolati, an progeniti ei corpore
choices.english: whether they were brought forth by word as the same, or begotten from his body
choices.why: Keeps the literal force of 'uerbo' (by word) and 'prolati' (brought forth) as distinct from 'progeniti' (begotten), preserving Mani's question about two possible modes of origin.
rejected: whether they were produced by the same word or begotten from his body
whether they came forth by word as one, or were begotten from his body

choices.why: Literal rendering of the idiom, preserving the source's emphasis on the truth's own state rather than smoothing it into 'as it really is.'
Keeps the adverb 'manifesto' as 'clearly' and the verb 'cognoscere' as 'to know,' preserving the distinction between knowing and believing that Augustine develops throughout.
Literal rendering of 'constitutio' as 'constitution,' preserving the cosmological sense of the world's establishment rather than using the more familiar biblical phrase 'foundation of the world.'

choices.english: to separate the nature of light and of darkness
choices.why: Keeps 'naturam' as 'nature' per the glossary and preserves the genitive construction 'of light and of darkness' rather than converting to adjectives.
rejected: to separate the light-nature and the darkness-nature
to distinguish the nature of light from that of darkness

choices.english: we cannot know as experienced and grasped
choices.why: Preserves the two participles 'expertam' (experienced) and 'conprehensam' (grasped) as distinct modes of knowledge, which is central to Augustine's contrast between belief and knowledge.
rejected: we cannot know by experience and comprehension
we cannot know it as something experienced and understood

pass_b_english: So then, he says, dearest brother Patticus, about what you indicated to me when you said you wanted to know what sort of birth Adam and Eve had—whether they were produced by word alone, or begotten from a body—I will answer you as is fitting. For this matter has been inserted and recorded in various scriptures and revelations by many people in dissimilar ways. Therefore the truth of this matter, as it has itself, is unknown by almost all nations, and by all who have even disputed long and much about it. For if clear knowledge of the generation of Adam and Eve had come about for them, they would never have been subject to corruption and death.

So he promises us clear knowledge of this matter, so that we will not be subjected to corruption and death. And if that is still not enough, see what follows. “Therefore,” he says, “many things must be mentioned beforehand so that one may arrive at this mystery without any ambiguity.” This is what I was saying: the truth must be shown to me in such a way that I may arrive at it without any ambiguity. Even if he himself did not promise it, I ought still to demand and insist on it, so that for so great a reward of evident and most certain knowledge I would not be ashamed to become a Manichaean from a Catholic Christian, no matter who contradicted me. So now let us hear what he brings forward.

“So if it seems good to you,” he says, “listen first to what existed before the constitution of the world and how the battle was waged, so that you may be able to separate the nature of light and of darkness.” Now he has proposed things that are unbelievable and entirely false. For who would believe that any battle was fought before the constitution of the world? And yet, even if it were believable, we should want not to believe, but to know. For someone who says that the Persians and Scythians fought a war with each other many years ago says something believable, but we can only believe it as something heard or read, not know it as experienced and grasped. Since I would reject him if he said something of that sort—for he did not promise things I would be forced to believe, but things I could know without any ambiguity—how shall I not reject him when he says things that are not only uncertain but even unbelievable? But what then? What if he makes them clear and known by some reasoning? Let us hear, then, if we can, with all patience and gentleness, what follows.

problems.quote: whether they were brought forth by word as the same
problems.why: "idem" means "the same" but modifies "they," not "word"; "prolati" means "produced/brought forth," not "brought forth as the same." The syntax is mangled.
problems.fix: whether they were produced by word alone, or begotten from his body

problems.quote: so that we may not be subject
problems.why: The subjunctive here expresses purpose/result of the promise, but "so that we may not be subject" misses that this is Mani's claimed outcome of knowing; "subiciamur" is present subjunctive, but context suggests future consequence.
problems.fix: so that we will not be subjected

problems.quote: we do not want merely to believe it now
problems.source_quote: modo nos non credere. sed cognoscere uelimus
problems.why: "modo" here means "only/merely" with "non credere" — "we do not want merely to believe, but to know." The English "now" misreads "modo" as temporal.
problems.fix: we do not want merely to believe, but to know

problems.quote: by almost all nations and by all
problems.source_quote: ab uniuersis fere gentibus ignoratur et ab omnibus. qui etiam de hoc diu multumque disputarunt
problems.why: The Latin has two groups: "by almost all nations" AND "by all who have disputed long about it." The English merges them confusingly, making "all" seem to modify "nations."
problems.fix: by almost all nations, and by all who have even disputed long and much about it
problems.ruling: 'ab omnibus. qui...disputarunt' = 'by all who disputed'; English 'by all' wrongly attaches to nations.

problems.why: "subiacerent" is imperfect subjunctive in a contrary-to-fact condition: "they would never HAVE BEEN subject." English "would never be" changes the temporal sense.
problems.fix: they would never have been subject to corruption and death
problems.ruling: 'subiacerent' imperfect subjunctive in contrary-to-fact: 'would never have been subject,' not 'would never be.'

edits.old: whether they were brought forth by word as the same, or begotten from his body
edits.new: whether they were produced by word alone, or begotten from his body

edits.old: so that we may not be subject to corruption and death
edits.new: so that we will not be subjected to corruption and death

edits.old: we do not want merely to believe it now, but to know it
edits.new: we do not want merely to believe, but to know

edits.old: by almost all nations and by all who have even disputed long and much about it
edits.new: by almost all nations, and by all who have even disputed long and much about it

edits.old: they would never be subject to corruption and death
edits.new: they would never have been subject to corruption and death

fixed: Fixed 'whether they were brought forth by word as the same' to 'whether they were produced by word alone, or begotten from his body': source 'utrum uerbo sint idem prolati' means 'whether they were produced by word as the same,' where 'idem' modifies 'they' and 'prolati' means 'produced.'

Fixed 'so that we may not be subject' to 'so that we will not be subjected': source 'ne corruptioni ac morti subiciamur' expresses the promised consequence of knowing, better rendered with future sense.

Fixed 'we do not want merely to believe it now, but to know it' to 'we do not want merely to believe, but to know': source 'modo nos non credere. sed cognoscere uelimus' uses 'modo' as 'merely,' not temporal 'now.'

Fixed 'by almost all nations and by all who have even disputed long and much about it' to 'by almost all nations, and by all who have even disputed long and much about it': source 'ab uniuersis fere gentibus ignoratur et ab omnibus. qui etiam de hoc diu multumque disputarunt' has two distinct groups; comma clarifies the separation.

Fixed 'they would never be subject' to 'they would never have been subject': source 'numquam corruptioni et morti subiacerent' is imperfect subjunctive in a contrary-to-fact condition, requiring past conditional in English.

problems.quote: we do not want merely to believe, but to know
problems.source_quote: modo nos non credere. sed cognoscere uelimus
problems.why: "modo" here means "only/merely" but the Latin structure is "non credere sed cognoscere uelimus" (we wish not to believe but to know). The English "merely" is misplaced—Augustine denies wanting to believe at all, not merely wanting to believe.
problems.fix: we wish not to believe, but to know

edits.old: we do not want merely to believe, but to know
edits.new: we wish not to believe, but to know

fixed: Changed 'we do not want merely to believe, but to know' to 'we wish not to believe, but to know': source 'modo nos non credere. sed cognoscere uelimus' means 'we wish not to believe but to know,' denying belief altogether, not merely wanting to believe.

problems.quote: we wish not to believe, but to know
problems.source_quote: modo nos non credere. sed cognoscere uelimus
problems.why: Wrong modality: 'uelimus' is jussive/subjunctive 'we should want/would want', not indicative 'we wish'.
problems.fix: we should want not to believe, but to know

problems.why: Latin 'ei' = 'to/for him' (Patticus); English 'his' wrongly makes Adam the referent.
problems.ruling: 'ei' dative singular, refers to Patticus (the one asking); 'his body' wrongly makes Adam the father, changing meaning.

problems.quote: So then, dearest brother Patticus, about what you indicated to me
problems.source_quote: De eo igitur, inquit, frater dilectissime Pattici, quod mihi significasti
problems.why: Missing 'inquit'—Mani's direct quotation not marked; reads as Augustine's words.
problems.fix: So then, he says, dearest brother Patticus, about what you indicated to me
problems.ruling: 'inquit' omitted; unmarked speaker shift misleads reader about voice attribution

edits.old: So then, dearest brother Patticus, about what you indicated to me
edits.new: So then, he says, dearest brother Patticus, about what you indicated to me

edits.old: we wish not to believe, but to know
edits.new: we should want not to believe, but to know

fixed: Added 'he says' to mark Mani's direct quotation, matching 'inquit' in the source.
Changed 'his body' to 'a body' because Latin 'ei corpore' means 'from a body' (dative of reference to Patticus), not 'from his [Adam's] body'.
Changed 'we wish' to 'we should want' because 'uelimus' is jussive/subjunctive, not indicative.

dismissed.quote: we should want not to believe, but to know
dismissed.why: "modo" here means "only/just," not "even if it were believable, we should want not to believe." Augustine says "we want not merely to believe but to know."
dismissed.note: Here 'modo nos non credere sed cognoscere uelimus' means we want to know rather than believe, and the English says that; the checker's 'not merely' softens Augustine's contrast.

last_rejected.why: Latin idiom for the truth as it really is; the calque is not intelligible English.
last_rejected.fix: Therefore the truth of this matter, as it really is, is unknown by almost all nations
last_rejected.ruling: "ut sese habet" rendered "as it has itself" is awkward calque, but meaning (as it stands) is recoverable; stylistic, not meaning-changing. Minor, not major.
